questions.question: What is time complexity and how do you reason about it in Ruby?
questions.title: Time Complexity Basics
questions.direct_answer: Time complexity describes how runtime grows with input size n. The big ones: O(1) constant (hash lookup, array index), O(log n) logarithmic (binary search), O(n) linear (each over an array), O(n log n) linearithmic (sort, sort_by), O(n^2) quadratic (nested each). You reason about Ruby code by counting loops: a single each is O(n); nested eaches are O(n^2); a hash lookup inside a loop keeps it O(n) (O(1) per lookup); sort is O(n log n). The goal is to pick the lowest complexity that fits — a hash turns an O(n^2) pair-finding loop into O(n).

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can name O(1)/O(log n)/O(n)/O(n log n)/O(n^2), count loops in Ruby, and pick the lower-complexity structure (hash for O(1)).
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Counting only outer loops (miss nested each as O(n^2)), or calling sort O(n) (it's O(n log n)).
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Time complexity = how runtime grows with n: O(1) hash lookup, O(log n) binary search, O(n) each, O(n log n) sort, O(n^2) nested each. Pick the lower-complexity structure.

sections.title: How Runtime Grows With n
sections.content: Time complexity describes how runtime grows with input size n. The big ones: O(1) constant — hash lookup, array index; O(log n) logarithmic — binary search; O(n) linear — each over an array; O(n log n) linearithmic — sort, sort_by; O(n^2) quadratic — nested each. You reason about Ruby code by counting loops: a single each is O(n); nested eaches are O(n^2); a hash lookup inside a loop keeps it O(n) because each lookup is O(1); sort is O(n log n). The goal is to pick the lowest complexity that fits — a hash turns an O(n^2) pair-finding nested loop into O(n) by giving O(1) lookup, which is the single most common optimization.

sections.title: Complexity Ladder
sections.content:
O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n^2).

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  C1[O(1) hash lookup] --> L[O(log n) binary search]
  L --> N[O(n) each]
  N --> NL[O(n log n) sort]
  NL --> Q[O(n^2) nested each]
```

sections.title: Reasoning about Ruby code
sections.content:
```ruby
# O(1) - hash lookup / array index
h = { a: 1 }; h[:a]          # constant time
arr = [1,2,3]; arr[0]        # constant time

# O(log n) - binary search (array must be sorted)
# arr.bsearch { |x| x >= target }

# O(n) - one each over the array
arr.each { |x| puts x }      # linear in arr.length
arr.sum                      # O(n)

# O(n log n) - sort / sort_by
arr.sort                    # n log n
arr.sort_by { |x| x.len }   # n log n

# O(n^2) - nested each (avoid!)
arr.each { |a| arr.each { |b| puts a + b } }   # n * n

# Hash turns O(n^2) pair-find into O(n):
# nested loop: for each x, scan for target-x  -> O(n^2)
# with seen hash: one pass, O(1) lookup each   -> O(n)
```

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Counting only the outer loop and missing a nested each (that's O(n^2)).
Calling sort O(n) — it's O(n log n), the dominant cost.
Using an O(n) include?/index inside a loop (O(n^2)); a hash makes it O(n).

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Time complexity = how runtime grows with input size n.
O(1) hash lookup/index; O(log n) binary search; O(n) each; O(n log n) sort; O(n^2) nested each.
Count loops: one each is O(n); nested eaches are O(n^2).
A hash lookup is O(1) — it turns an O(n^2) pair loop into O(n).
sort/sort_by is O(n log n), not O(n) — the dominant cost.
